item.title: What will it take for India’s fintech infrastructure to go global?
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Movin Jain of Skydo and Srijon Biswas of PhonePe discussed building payments infrastructure at scale, the challenges of cross-border transactions, and how AI could change business operations.
item.content:encoded:
India’s payments ecosystem has shown that financial infrastructure can operate at enormous scale. But as fintech companies expand into cross-border business payments and adopt AI, they face a different set of challenges.

At TechSparks 2026, Movin Jain, Founder of Skydo, and Srijon Biswas, Chief Technology Officer at PhonePe, discussed the technology behind large-scale payments, the need for transparency in cross-border transactions, and the opportunities emerging from AI.

The panel, titled ‘From domestic scale to global rails: The evolution of India's fintech infrastructure’, was moderated by Priya Patankar, Head of Corporate Communications at PhonePe.

Cross-border payments: A market still in its early stages

Jain believes cross-border payments offer considerable opportunities because fintech adoption remains relatively low.

India exports goods and services worth approximately $850 billion annually and imports around $1 trillion worth, with both figures growing. However, less than 10% of these transactions are handled by fintech companies, according to Jain. Banks continue to manage most of these payments.

Skydo focuses on business-to-business (B2B) payments, where fintech adoption is even lower than in consumer payments. Many businesses are still learning that fintech companies can help them manage cross-border transactions.

Jain believes the immediate opportunity lies in building awareness of the category rather than competing on price.

“Spending time worrying about other fintech players and how to compete with them is not a good use of time. That time will come maybe 5–10 years down the line when all of us have a lot more penetration in the market,” he said.

For now, the priority is to show businesses how fintech companies can address payment problems they have traditionally relied on banks to solve.

While venture capital activity and regulatory developments have helped the sector progress, Jain believes there is considerable room for growth.

Building technology that can scale

PhonePe’s experience shows the importance of making the right architectural decisions early.

Biswas said the company planned for scale from the beginning. Its early architects established systems and engineering practices that continued to serve the platform as it grew by nearly 100-1,000X. 

“It's the same pattern that we have used, same set of libraries, same set of constructs that we have used. So it’s been ingrained from the very beginning. We haven’t actually done a large refactor of our architecture for the longest that I can remember,” he said.

Rather than undertake a major architectural overhaul, PhonePe has focused on understanding its technology stack and making deliberate choices about the systems it uses.

The company built its own site reliability engineering (SRE) team, adopted a sharded database architecture from the outset, and chose technologies that its engineers understood well.

Biswas also emphasized the importance of engineering hygiene, instrumentation, testing, quality assurance, and scale testing.

At PhonePe’s scale, even unlikely failures can become operational problems. Biswas recalled encountering bugs that had surfaced at another organization years earlier.

Building for scale, he said, requires more than increasing capacity. It also depends on sound architecture, careful technology choices, and the ability to understand and manage systems under demanding conditions.

Managing India's scale and diversity

Biswas said regulation is not necessarily a constraint for fintech companies. It can encourage businesses to establish the right practices from the beginning.

The bigger engineering challenge, he explained, comes from India's combination of scale and diversity.

He compared India's scale with China’s, while pointing out that differences across geographies, use cases, and merchant environments create additional complexity.

PhonePe encountered this during its early expansion into offline payments.

While integrating with merchants, including pharmacy chains such as Apollo Pharmacy, the company found that different systems were already in use across states and cities.

Supporting these merchants meant building integrations for multiple systems rather than relying on a single standardized setup.

These differences create numerous exceptions and edge cases that must be managed alongside high transaction volumes.

Patankar also noted that PhonePe had received its UAE licence, bringing new opportunities and challenges.

Biswas said the company would need to adapt its infrastructure for international markets rather than simply replicate its Indian operations.

Much of PhonePe’s existing payments architecture has been designed specifically for India. The company is now exploring additional layers of abstraction that could make international expansion easier without having to deploy the entire existing stack and build large teams in every new market.

Why transparency matters in cross-border payments

For businesses receiving payments from overseas clients, speed and cost are not the only concerns.

Jain believes transparency is equally important.

Small businesses, freelancers, and service providers may know how many dollars a client has transferred and how many rupees eventually reach their accounts. However, they may not understand the exchange rate used, the foreign exchange charges, or how the final amount was calculated.

Without this information, businesses may find it difficult to question charges or compare payment providers.

Jain said Skydo is working to educate customers about these costs and help them understand where savings are possible.

He gave the example of a business receiving a $5,000 payment from an international client.

In a transparent system, the business would know as soon as the client makes the payment how many rupees it can expect to receive and when the money is likely to arrive.

It would also be able to see the prevailing exchange rate, understand how the final amount was calculated, and know the applicable GST.

How AI could change business operations

The discussion also covered AI’s growing role in fintech and its potential impact on businesses.

Jain said Skydo works with service businesses ranging from legal and consulting firms to IT services companies and freelancers.

He believes AI agents and automation could allow smaller firms to provide services that previously required the resources of much larger organizations.

This could create opportunities for smaller, specialized businesses and freelancers to earn more than was previously possible, particularly in India.

At PhonePe, Biswas described AI adoption across three areas: user-facing experiences, developer productivity, and operational efficiency.

In the PhonePe app, users can search and ask questions about their transactions using a model running at the edge.

AI is also being used in operational workflows to interpret regulatory and compliance documents. It helps teams understand what regulatory changes mean for the business without having to manually process every document.

Developer productivity is another area where PhonePe has seen improvements.

Biswas said AI-assisted coding has reduced some processes that previously took three to five days to around 15 minutes.

Test-case generation has become 5-6X faster in certain cases, while some customer experience and support workflows have also recorded savings of 5-6X.

However, Biswas emphasized that automation does not eliminate the need for human oversight.

In a regulated business, workflows that could affect users, systems, or processes will continue to require a human in the loop.

Taking India’s payments infrastructure global

India already has several foundational elements in place, including payments infrastructure and systems related to identity and consent.

Biswas believes these provide an advantage as the fintech sector evolves.

However, cross-border payments remain structurally complex.

There is no single central counterparty connecting all central banks and currencies through a unified ledgering system. Businesses must therefore navigate a fragmented payments infrastructure, creating problems that fintech companies are trying to solve.

For India’s fintech sector, the next challenge is to build on the strengths of its domestic infrastructure while adapting to international markets.

That will involve making cross-border payments more transparent, managing the complexity of different markets, and using AI to improve business productivity.

item.title: Discover how Superminis, Nayam by Lakshita and Broadstar are scaling nationally with Myntra’s platform capabilities
item.description:
From kidswear to ethnic and western wear, Superminis, Nayam by Lakshita, and Broadstar are using trend reports and events like BFF to enhance their offerings and reach more shoppers across the country.
Myntra’s Big Fashion Festival (BFF) gives brands an opportunity to reach shoppers across India.
item.content:encoded:
Myntra’s Big Fashion Festival (BFF) gives brands an opportunity to reach shoppers across India. This year, the event features 21,000 emerging brands and labels, including 13,000 participating for the first time, and more than eight million styles, twice the selection of the previous edition. Brands also have access to Myntra’s 80 million-plus monthly active users, technology, creator ecosystem and nationwide reach.

Three brands, Super Minis, Nayam by Lakshita and Broadstar, share how the platform has helped them expand their customer base by reaching a much wider audience.

Superminis: Understanding what parents want

Founded by Amandeep Singh in 2019, Superminis was launched to help parents find soft, comfortable clothing for their children in the right sizes. The kidswear brand joined Myntra in 2022. Singh says Myntra’s category insights, feedback on what’s working and what’s not, have helped Superminis improve its products and enable the team to plan its assortment, while brand-building recommendations have played a key role in winning customer trust and love. During marquee events like BFF and the End of Reason Sale (EORS), Superminis sees sales increase 1.2–1.5X compared with regular business days. Rakhi 2025 was particularly a highlight for the brand.

“Rakhi 2025 was the standout moment where our ethnic wear sales on Myntra exceeded our entire previous month’s revenue. That increase in traction during events is made possible because Myntra attracts shoppers who truly appreciate quality,” Singh says.

Nayam by Lakshita: Using data to guide design

Nayam is part of Lakshita’s established ethnic wear business. Drawing on years of experience in understanding women’s clothing preferences, the brand focuses on fit, premium fabrics, and comfortable styling.

To expand its reach, Nayam launched on Myntra in September 2023. Access to ethnic wear shopping trends helped the team make more informed business decisions. Nayam improved its assortment planning, identified opportunities in new categories and made decisions based on shopping preferences.

The Partner Portal is among the brand’s most-used tools. Its performance metrics help the team identify areas for improvement and make decisions about product design and visibility, combining its industry experience with shopping behaviour.

Major shopping events have also helped Nayam reach thousands of new customers, including those outside its local markets.

For Suneet Kharbanda, Managing Director of Nayam by Lakshita, customer expectations play an important role in product development.

“Myntra shoppers are very aware of what they are buying. They look at the fabric, fit, styling, reviews, and value before making a decision. That inspires us to raise the bar to keep up with such thoughtful shoppers,” he says.

Broadstar: Turning insights into new collections

Broadstar began with women’s western wear, focusing on trend-led designs, good fits, and competitive pricing. After establishing itself in the category, the brand expanded into men’s casual wear.

It joined Myntra in 2021 to reach a wider audience. Since then, the insights have helped Broadstar understand shopper preferences and expand its product range.

The brand now offers more than 4,200 lifestyle styles and uses Myntra’s trend analytics to identify opportunities for new collections.

Major shopping events such as BFF and EORS have also contributed to growth, with sales increasing 1.5–1.8X during these periods.

Broadstar uses Myntra’s growth dashboard and data and insight tools to plan inventory and bring new styles to market faster. It helps the team understand what customers are looking for and make better decisions about its product selection.

The brand also values its access to shoppers who pay close attention to fashion and product quality. Their expectations encourage Broadstar to improve its products while exploring opportunities to expand.

For Super Minis, Nayam by Lakshita, and Broadstar, overall insights have become an important part of business planning. Superminis uses the data to improve its kidswear assortment, Nayam to guide ethnic wear designs, and Broadstar to expand its product selection.

From managing units and improving fulfilment to identifying trends and developing products, these brands are using Myntra’s tools to plan their next stage of growth.

item.title: Beyond transactions: How PhonePe and Razorpay are using AI to improve digital payments
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Deep Agrawal of PhonePe and Khilan Haria of Razorpay discussed how contextual payments and AI can improve customer experiences, make financial services more accessible, and help small businesses grow.
item.content:encoded:
India has made digital payments as simple as scanning a QR code. The next opportunity lies in using payments to connect consumers with relevant financial products and help businesses address the challenges of growing online.

At TechSparks 2026, Deep Agrawal, Head of Payments at PhonePe, and Khilan Haria, Chief Product Officer at Razorpay, joined Madanmohan Rao, Research Director at YourStory, for a panel discussion titled ‘Beyond transactions: Solving financial inclusion with contextual money’.

The discussion covered how payments are becoming part of a wider digital experience, from improving transaction success rates to helping merchants attract and retain customers.

Beyond payments: What do users and businesses need?

Agrawal said digital payments have become part of everyday life for more than 500 million UPI users, who use the system to send money to friends, pay electricity bills, shop online, and make payments at stores.

However, the next challenge is to bring another 500 million people into the digital payments ecosystem while helping existing users access financial products beyond payments.

For businesses, accepting payments is only the first step.

Haria said Razorpay’s experience working with millions of small and medium businesses has shown that merchants face several challenges once they have the infrastructure to collect payments, including attracting customers, improving conversions, and encouraging repeat purchases.

“Over the years, we’ve learned as we’ve worked with millions of these SMBs. The larger problem sometimes goes beyond payments. Payments is what I now call the core infrastructure that SMBs need to set up their digital commerce or online business. But beyond that, the struggle most businesses go through is ‘how do I get demand? How do I maximize retention? How do I uplift conversion?’” he said.

Razorpay initially addressed some of these requirements through products for payroll, salary disbursements, and vendor payments.

However, conversations with merchants showed that businesses needed support beyond managing money. They also needed help building and growing their online operations.

Haria said helping more small businesses establish an online presence and succeed in digital commerce could contribute to the growth of India's digital economy.

Using transaction data to improve payments

Every digital transaction generates information that payment platforms can use to better understand customer needs, identify risks and improve the payment experience.

Haria discussed Razorpay's transaction-led foundation model, Vulcan 5.2, which is designed to understand what he described as the language of payments.

According to Haria, each transaction contains nearly 3,000 attributes. By analyzing these, the model can predict missing information, assess the likelihood of fraud, and determine whether a transaction is likely to convert.

This can help businesses identify suspicious transactions, reduce risks, and improve the chances of converting potential buyers into paying customers.

Haria explained that conventional machine learning typically involves identifying patterns, developing hypotheses, and training models around them. Transformer-based models, however, can identify smaller patterns that may be difficult to detect through conventional approaches.

At PhonePe, machine learning is being used to make payments more reliable.

Agrawal discussed an internal model called Kill Switch, which predicts whether a transaction is likely to succeed. It considers factors such as bank response times and recent transaction success rates to assess the likelihood of a successful payment.

“Consumers don't really care whether a transaction fails. What they care about is it should not go into a pending state,” Agrawal said.

“In this model, we tell the customer even before they initiate the transaction that your bank is probably down, come back and do the transaction later.”

Agrawal said this approach helps build trust and encourages users to return to the platform.

Transaction context can also help payment platforms recommend financial products based on customer needs.

For example, a customer booking an international flight through PhonePe may benefit from a travel insurance recommendation. For someone who travels only within India, a bus booking may be more relevant.

Agrawal said PhonePe uses guardrails in its algorithms to avoid recommending products that are not relevant to individual customers.

Razorpay: From AI assistants to autonomous agents

Razorpay is also using AI to help merchants manage everyday business operations.

Haria discussed two initiatives, Ray and Agent Studio, designed to make business support and automation more accessible.

Ray is an AI assistant that functions as an account manager for businesses. While larger customers typically have dedicated account managers, providing similar support to smaller merchants has been difficult to scale.

Ray aims to address this gap by allowing merchants to explain their problems through WhatsApp voice notes or messages in plain English, without navigating complex dashboards and consoles.

Agent Studio goes further by allowing businesses to use autonomous AI agents for specific tasks.

These include recovering abandoned shopping carts, representing merchants in disputes, confirming cash-on-delivery orders and verifying delivery addresses.

Haria said Razorpay had 12 agents live, with 600 brands using them, including some that use multiple agents.

The company plans to increase the number of agents to 100 over the next six months and eventually reach 100,000 businesses using them.

PhonePe: Bringing more users into digital payments

Agrawal also discussed how AI-powered tools could help bring more people into the digital payments ecosystem.

He highlighted the challenges faced by feature-phone users, many of whom live in smaller towns and rural areas or are beginning to participate in the formal economy.

Feature phones have several limitations, including the inability to receive software updates over the air. Users may also need assistance with processes that are familiar to more digitally experienced consumers.

To address these challenges, PhonePe has introduced voice bots that help users with tasks such as linking bank accounts and setting up UPI PINs.

PhonePe is also working to make it easier for micro and small merchants to start selling online.

Building a website using platforms such as Shopify or WooCommerce can be expensive and complicated for young entrepreneurs.

PhonePe's SmartPages product aims to simplify this process by allowing merchants to create a checkout page, list products, and start selling without hiring a web developer or subscribing to a more complex platform.

India's digital payments ecosystem has made everyday transactions easier for millions of people. The next opportunity, according to Agrawal and Haria, lies in using that infrastructure to address a wider range of consumer and business needs.

From improving payment reliability and providing relevant financial products to helping merchants manage operations and reach customers, contextual payments and AI could extend the role of payment platforms beyond transactions.

item.title: As chip prices surge, EV maker Ultraviolette is working on ways to absorb costs
item.description: Bengaluru-based Ultraviolette—which produces high-performance electric motorcycles—says it will not pass on the input costs to customers.
item.content:encoded:
The global shortage of memory chips has driven up costs, placing a huge strain on electric vehicle makers in the country.

Bengaluru-based Ultraviolette—which produces high-performance electric motorcycles—says it will not pass on the high input costs to customers and is exploring other ways to tide over the situation. 

Memory chips are a critical component of an electric vehicle, used to store data, run control software, and manage real-time operations across critical systems. 

According to Ultraviolette’s Founder and CTO, Niraj Rajmohan, RAM (random access memory) alone adds Rs 20,000 to the cost of a vehicle. With global companies building very large data centres, there has been a surge in memory chip consumption, he added. 

AI data centres are projected to consume 70% of global memory chip production in 2026. The data centre boom has led to a supply crunch, subsequently shoring up costs of chips. 

But it would not be fair to pass on the costs to customers, said Rajmohan, adding that a threefold jump in memory prices in recent times cannot translate into a threefold jump in the price of an electric bike, and customers cannot be asked to suddenly pay far more. 

The company is working on alternatives to absorb costs. 

For now, Ultraviolette is scouting for alternative parts, including software, components and technologies, and alternative manufacturers to partner with. 

The company is also relying on partners who hold a stake in the company, including TVS, TDK Ventures, and Intel, for their knowhow and expertise, said Rajmohan. He, however, did not elaborate on the alternatives. 

Rajmohan was speaking at the launch of X-47 Venom, Ultraviolette’s first bike built on its new platform ‘VX-100’.

What is VX-100?

VX-100 is a 100V electric powertrain architecture that seeks to improve performance and efficiency in electric two-wheelers. 

An electric powertrain architecture is the integrated system of energy storage, electronics, and mechanical components that converts stored electrical energy into mechanical motion to propel the vehicle.

Rather than upgrading the parts one at a time, Ultraviolette has redesigned the battery, motor, and control electronics together, as one system.

The X-47 Venom is the first bike built on this new architecture. The company claims it offers better battery cooling, lighter components, and stronger power delivery, along with support for DC fast charging at up to 12 kW. 

Most electric two-wheelers run on 48V, said Rajmohan, adding that the telecom industry and Southeast Asian manufacturers built their systems around it. 

At 100V, X-47 Venom’s system draws lower current, and hence produces less heat. The objective is to provide high speed and better performance without the heat, energy loss, and extra weight that usually come with electric vehicles. 

Currently, Qualcomm supplies the chips that power the bike's new dashboard, while TDK provides the RF (radio frequency) components and capacitors. 

The X-47 Venom is priced at Rs 2,65,000 for the first 5,000 buyers. Bookings opened on October 22, and deliveries are set to start in November. The European launch will happen on November 3 at EICMA, an international motorcycle expo in Milan.

The bike has undergone extensive test rides covering 150 to 200 km a day for several months, said Rajmohan. 

Ultraviolette’s product portfolio includes the F77 sports bike that is targeted at sports enthusiasts, while the X-47 Crossover is intended to appeal to a broader set of customers, including sports, adventure and street riders. The Crossover makes up about 90% of the company’s sales. 

The new VX-100 platform will go into all of Ultraviolette’s forthcoming products. Four launches are expected next year, including the Tesseract (a scooter) and Shockwave (an Enduro motorcycle), and an upgraded F77 bike. 

Roughly 90% of sales come from India and 10% from abroad, including the European market, where the company has been expanding. There are more than 7,000 Ultraviolette bikes on the roads worldwide today. 

Ultraviolette was founded in 2016 by Narayan Subramaniam and Niraj Rajmohan. Its backers include Lingotto, TDK Ventures, Qualcomm Ventures, Zoho Corporation, TVS Motors, Yali Capital, and Speciale Invest.

Edited by Swetha Kannan

item.title: [Weekly funding roundup Oct 17-23] VC funding falls below $100M amid lack of big deals
item.description: Venture capital funding in the third week of October recorded a sharp fall due to lower number of deals and absence of large value transactions.
item.content:encoded:
Venture capital funding for Indian startups saw a steep decline in the third week of October, primarily due to a lower number of deals and the absence of any large-value transactions.

Venture capital funding during the week stood at just $96 million across 15 deals. In contrast, startups raised a total of $180 million in the previous week.

This sharp drop in venture capital funding highlights the challenges the Indian startup ecosystem continues to face in raising a steady flow of capital. This is also the eighth time so far this year that weekly venture capital funding has fallen below the $100 million mark.

The only large deal during the week was Even Healthcare’s $50 million raise. The other deals were worth $11 million or less. While transactions during the week saw investors place their bets across segments such as healthcare, consumer and AI, there were no other significant deals.

The biggest challenge for the Indian startup ecosystem so far this year has been the low number of large-value deals. In fact, there have been just 16 deals worth $100 million or more. This does not bode well for the ecosystem as 2026 draws to a close.

However, there is hope for a revival in 2027.

Key transactions

Even Healthcare raised $50 million from Khosla Ventures and Alpha Wave.

The Pant Project, a premium menswear label, raised Rs 109 crore ($11.4 million approx.) from Mirae Asset Venture Investments, Sorin Investments, Alteria Capital, and family offices.

Rural healthcare platform CureBay raised Rs 100 crore ($10.4 million approx.) from IvyCap Ventures, Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners.

Chapter Home, a home and kitchen consumer brand, raised Rs 63 crore ($6.6 million approx.) from Bessemer Venture Partners, Stride Ventures, influencer Tanmay Bhat, and select family offices.

Traveltech startup TravClan raised $5 million from Flipkart, August One, and Trifecta Capital.

AI startup Hunar AI raised Rs 40 crore ($4.2 million) from Blume Ventures, Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures and startup founders.

item.title: Gen Z is shaping India’s beauty market: prevention first,and going beyond the metros
item.description:
Subtitle: For this generation, beauty is prevention first with sun protection products seeing a 60% growth among Gen Z shoppers, finds a new report titled ‘Beauty in the age of Gen Z’ by Myntra.
Gen Z is changing how India shops for beauty. For this generation, beauty is part of how they show u
item.content:encoded:
Gen Z is changing how India shops for beauty. For this generation, beauty is part of how they show up every day. They protect their skin before fixing it and try premium brands through minis, and they are taking beauty well beyond the metros. These are among the findings of 'Beauty in the Age of Gen Z', a new report released by Myntra, which finds a generation that chooses ingredients over hype.

Gen Z and millennials are both growing the beauty and personal care category on Myntra, with Gen Z giving the category a 75% higher share of its wallet. Self-expression comes first for this generation, and the category is one of the clearest places it shows. Gen Z’s beauty and personal care spend per customer is up 1.2X YoY alongside a fast growing customer base on Myntra. Half of Gen Z’s beauty buyers on Myntra live in Tier II and III cities. Sun protection (SPF) products are up 60% YoY among Gen Z shoppers, while 53% of luxe makeup orders on Myntra now include a mini.

Deepak Joshi, Senior Director, Beauty and Personal Care, Myntra, said, “This is a skin-first generation. Gen Z doesn’t use a brand name as a shortcut for trust. They want to understand what’s in the product and what it will do for their skin. They keep their routines short and choose what works, and they think proactively, preventing damage instead of fixing it later. That’s why sun protection has stopped being a seasonal purchase for them. It’s a year-round habit.”

Gen Z is shaping a market that industry reports* expect to grow from ~$23 billion to ~$40 billion. India still spends only ~$15 per head on beauty, against $38 in China and $383 in the US, according to industry estimates by Redseer.

Sharon Pais, Head of Myntra, said, “Beauty and personal care is one of Myntra’s strongest growth engines. For Gen Z, beauty is self-expression. It’s how they show up, plan their looks, and live their social lives. They try premium and international brands through minis, find new ones through creators and K-Beauty, and choose on ingredients and efficacy, in cities across the country. The brands that win will meet this shopper early, make discovery easy, and earn trust through the product and its ingredients.”

Key findings

Minis and creators: Minis make up 14% of luxe units sold, led by lipstick, perfume and face primer. Brands such as M.A.C, Kayali, Smashbox, and Salvatore Ferragamo get more than half of their new customers through minis. Video is how Gen Z finds beauty. Myntra has ~82,000 active beauty creators, UGC beauty content is up 40% YoY, and nearly two in three new beauty creator registrations over the last four months are Gen Z.

Beyond the metros: Gen Z baskets in Tier II and III cities include serums, toners, sunscreens, and hair masks alongside everyday staples. These cities account for half of the platform's international beauty demand. Ludhiana, Patna, Bhopal, Indore, Guwahati, Surat, Varanasi, and Imphal are among the cities driving growth.

Prevention, ingredients, and K-Beauty: Sun protection has become a year-round habit among Gen Z shoppers, with searches up 80% for spray sunscreens, 70% for ingredient-led sunscreens and 60% for tinted sunscreens (SPF, or sun protection factor). Gel-based, fragrance-free, and non-sticky textures are in demand, and Gen Z is seeking out ingredients such as Centella asiatica, copper peptides, azelaic acid, and panthenol.

K-Beauty demand grew 200% YoY and searches rose more than 300%. Myntra now offers 1,000+ SKUs from 90+ K-Beauty brands, with 30+ added in the last year. Hair masks grew 110%, against 59% for conditioners, and men's skincare orders grew 78% YoY, led by Gen Z.

Repeat shoppers: Repeat Gen Z orders on Myntra are up ~70% this year, and the repeat beauty shopper and the repeat apparel shopper are more often than not the same person. Beauty, roughly 1 in 5 units ordered on Myntra, is growing at twice the online beauty market, and brought in nearly half a million new customers in May 2026 alone. Myntra offers ~2.5 lakh styles from 4,500+ brands, including 360+ international brands. Virtual Try-On makes shoppers 2X more likely to buy, and Skin Analyzer lifts conversion by ~58%. Beauty on M-Now spans ~600 brands, with delivery as quick as nine minutes.

Backing Indian brands: Myntra hosts 700 pure-play D2C beauty brands and 3,000 emerging D2C names, and D2C beauty has grown 68% so far in FY26. Plum, Minimalist, Foxtale, The Derma Co., and Chemist at Play are among those driving growth. Gen Z is 25% more likely to try an indigenous or D2C brand. Gen Z and millennial shoppers are both backing these brands, with Gen Z among the quickest to try them.

Deepash Jain, VP – Marketing, Myntra, added, “Gen Z doesn’t search to shop, they scroll to discover. That changes everything for us, from the platform experience to the brands we bring in to what happens after purchase. Marketing at Myntra has always been about following the customer. We have opened up our creator ecosystem so anyone with a community can talk about products they believe in. Trends find their way organically, and we don’t try to manufacture them.”

Gen Z's wishlist already points to what's next, including lactic acid, tranexamic acid, and foundation-SPF hybrids. Myntra's focus moves to scale and share, with a better pre- and post-purchase experience, a stronger ecosystem through Myntra GlamStream, and continued momentum in D2C, luxury, international beauty, non-metros and first-time online beauty shoppers.

The report was unveiled at the Myntra Beauty IRL event in Mumbai, alongside a panel discussion on The New Indian Beauty Consumer. It is based on the company's platform data, buying behaviour, and search trends from August 2025 to August 2026, covering Gen Z shoppers.

item.title: Rs 10,000 Cr into restaurants. But why do 80% fail? Here's the Hotshare F&B investment playbook
item.description: In this episode of the Prime Venture Partners Podcast, Lavanya, Founder, Hotshare, an F&B investment platform, explains what she looks for before funding a restaurant. The founder of burger brand ‘Beyondburg’, one of Hotshare’s portfolio companies, joins the podcast to share the brand's journey.
item.content:encoded:
India's restaurant industry is attracting serious capital, but building a profitable restaurant remains one of the most difficult businesses to crack. According to Lavanya Jayashankar, Founder and CEO of Hotshare, an F&B investment platform, around Rs 10,000 crore was deployed into the F&B business in 2025, while organised food services are expected to account for more than half the market by 2030.

Yet, despite growing consumer demand and investor interest, Lavanya points to an uncomfortable statistic: 80% of restaurants close within their first five years.

Hotshare funds restaurant businesses with a range of Rs 50 lakh to Rs 5 crore. For the investment platform, which raises capital for profitable restaurants and bars at the outlet level, the opportunity is not necessarily to change that statistic, but to identify and fund the businesses that have already demonstrated their ability to survive.

"My play here is to say, let's identify those 20," says Lavanya.

One example is Beyondburg, one of Hotshare’s portfolio companies. The burger brand began in Bengaluru in 2017 as a four-seater kiosk selling 40 to 50 burgers daily. Today, according to co-founder Mohammed Anas, the brand sells approximately 3,000 burgers a day and has just opened its sixth location 

Its journey offers a practical illustration of what Lavanya believes separates a successful restaurant from an attractive but financially unsustainable concept.

The Rs 50 lakh to Rs 5 crore funding gap

India's F&B industry has traditionally attracted two types of capital: institutional investors backing large, scalable chains and informal investors financing individual restaurants through personal networks.

Lavanya believes a significant opportunity exists between these two categories.

"There is a vast middle of profitable, successful entrepreneurs who are under-capitalized," she says, arguing that investors frequently evaluate restaurant businesses using frameworks borrowed from technology and direct-to-consumer companies.

The distinction is fundamental. A restaurant chain can create enterprise value through expansion, but an individual outlet generates value primarily through its operating cash flows.

Hotshare therefore evaluates outlets as income-generating assets rather than businesses dependent on a future acquisition or exit.

According to Lavanya, opening a restaurant typically requires Rs 50 lakh to Rs 5 crore, an amount that can be too small for institutional investors but substantial enough to demand professional financial oversight.

She says Hotshare's selected outlets offer a projected 15% to 20% post-tax internal rate of return over five to seven years, with returns distributed through profit sharing. She also describes the possibility of higher effective returns when investors reinvest those distributions, although these remain investment projections rather than guaranteed outcomes.

Why great food is not enough

For Lavanya, the economics of running a restaurant are more important than its popularity.

She outlines specific financial benchmarks across restaurant formats. Quick-service restaurants should aim for food costs below 18% of revenue, manpower costs below 15% and EBITDA margins above 18%. Casual dining restaurants can accommodate food costs of 18% to 22%, but should still target EBITDA margins exceeding 15%.

Rent is another critical variable.

"Whatever category you are in, it's not great business if your rent is more than 12 to 15% of your revenue," she explains.

These numbers help explain why a restaurant with excellent food, strong social media visibility, and crowded tables can still struggle financially.

Lavanya believes first-time founders frequently spend too much on their initial outlet before establishing product-market fit. A restaurant requiring Rs 5 crore in capital expenditure is not necessarily better positioned than one requiring Rs 2 crore. It may simply be a more expensive experiment.

Beyondburg followed a different approach.

Beyondburg: From 50 to 3,000 burgers a day

Anas recalls arriving in Bengaluru on a holiday and meeting his future co-founders, Ajmal and Nishaf. Together, they decided to start a small burger business near Christ College in Koramangala.

"We used to do, uh, 40 to 50 burgers a day," he recalls.

The founders operated the kiosk for almost three years before deciding to rebuild Beyondburg as a scalable brand, beginning with a flagship outlet in Calicut.

Rather than attempting to establish a large restaurant chain immediately, the team used its initial years to understand the product, customer preferences and operating requirements.

Lavanya considers this approach one of Beyondburg's biggest strengths.

"They didn't start with a five crore capex," she says, explaining how the founders first tested the concept before committing to larger outlets.

By the time Beyondburg began expanding, it had already invested in central procurement, vendor relationships and operational systems.

For Lavanya, the brand demonstrated that expansion could follow operational readiness rather than precede it.

Why Beyondburg refuses to sell pasta

Anas identifies three priorities behind Beyondburg's growth: product, people and operations.

Despite customer requests to introduce additional dishes, the company has resisted expanding beyond its core burger proposition.

"If they want to try pasta, they can go to somewhere else, right?" he says.

The decision is not simply about brand positioning. Every additional menu item introduces complexity into procurement, inventory, kitchen operations and service.

Beyondburg has instead focused on reducing unnecessary stock-keeping units and improving kitchen throughput, particularly during busy weekends.

Anas explains that the company works with kitchen consultants to estimate peak demand and design its outlets accordingly. At the Bengaluru location in Indiranagar where the podcast was recorded, he says the business sells 700 to 800 burgers a day.

The company has also built a structured approach to training. New employees are paired with experienced colleagues, while a dedicated trainer travels between outlets to maintain consistency.

The challenge, Anas explains, is ensuring that a growing business delivers the same product and customer experience regardless of location.

What made Beyondburg investable?

Lavanya first met Anas in December 2024, when Hotshare was still developing its investment framework.

Beyondburg subsequently became one of its portfolio brands, and she credits the business with helping shape Hotshare's evaluation checklist.

"Gold standard of operations data was available from day one," she explains.

The company maintained historical financial information, treated outlet-level profitability as non-negotiable and developed central systems before they were essential for its existing scale.

Its vendor relationships were also designed to support future expansion rather than simply meet immediate requirements.

But Lavanya's conviction was not built on financial information alone.

During her first visit to Beyondburg, before meeting Anas, she noticed that her water glass was consistently refilled without asking. At the end of the meal, employees offered a complimentary dessert without seeking management approval.

For her, these were indicators of a culture in which employees understood hospitality and had the freedom to improve customer experiences.

The combination of financial discipline, repeatable operations, and service quality made Beyondburg particularly attractive.

The real test of restaurant success

Lavanya believes the restaurant industry's next phase of growth will require founders and investors to rethink how they define success.

Opening more outlets is not necessarily evidence of a stronger business. A restaurant that expands rapidly while sacrificing profitability may ultimately destroy value rather than create it.

Beyondburg's experience illustrates an alternative approach: establish demand with limited capital, build operating systems, maintain product focus and expand only when the underlying economics support it.

For aspiring restaurateurs, Lavanya also emphasises the importance of working with experienced operators rather than assuming that culinary ability translates into business expertise.

"Hospitality is an execution business, it is not an ideas business," she says.

Beyondburg's journey from a four-seater kiosk to thousands of burgers a day shows why that distinction matters. The visible success is a popular consumer brand. Behind it are years of disciplined decisions about costs, people, procurement, kitchens and profitability.

For Hotshare, those are precisely the businesses worth backing.

item.title: PM inaugurates RBI's Rs 169-cr data centre, Cybersecurity Training Institute in Odisha
item.description: The data centre will host mission-critical payment and settlement systems, along with other flagship initiatives, the government said in a statement.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Reserve Bank of India's Rs 169-crore data centre and Cybersecurity Training Institute in Bhubaneswar on Sunday, officials said.

Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra, Odisha Governor Brajmohan Ram, Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi, Union Tribal Affairs Minister Jual Oram, and Deputy CMs Kanak Vardhan Singh Deo and Pravati Parida were also present.

The RBI's facility spans 18.55 acres at Info Valley-II in Jatni, and then RBI governor Shaktikanta Das laid the foundation stone on March 22, 2023.

The data centre will host mission-critical payment and settlement systems, along with other flagship initiatives, the government said in a statement.

It will help widen the reach, efficiency, and reliability of digital financial services and will form the secure digital foundation on which India's increasingly technology-driven financial economy can grow, it said.

Similarly, the Cybersecurity Training Institute will boost capability building, providing a dedicated institutional platform for cybersecurity and enterprise-technology training, research, and sector-wide capability development, it said.

The site was chosen for its geographical stability, away from seismically active zones and high-risk international border areas, reducing exposure to natural disasters and geopolitical vulnerabilities, an official said.

Majhi, in a social media post, said the data centre will add to Odisha's journey of development.

He said this was the PM's ninth visit to Odisha after the formation of the BJP government in the state in 2024.

Majhi said the Jatni data centre will be the second of its kind after the one in Navi Mumbai.

The facilities have been designed to meet the bank's computing requirements and provide a secure, resilient, scalable and future-ready computing ecosystem for the bank and the broader financial sector, officials said.

item.title: 5 Lessons to learn from Nexus by Yuval Noah Harari
item.description: Discover five key lessons from Yuval Noah Harari’s Nexus on information, power, artificial intelligence and how networks shape society.
item.content:encoded:
Information has always shaped human civilisation. From ancient stories and religious texts to newspapers, television and social media, the way people share information influences what they believe, how they make decisions and whom they trust.

In Nexus, historian and author Yuval Noah Harari examines how information networks have shaped human history and how they may influence our future. Published in 2024, the book explores the relationship between information, power, truth and the development of artificial intelligence.

Harari challenges the assumption that having more information automatically makes societies wiser or better informed.

What matters is how information is organised, who controls it and whether the systems that distribute it help people correct their mistakes. Here are five important lessons to learn from Nexus and how they apply to the world we live in today.

5 Lessons to learn from Nexus by Yuval Noah Harari

1. More information does not always mean more truth

One of the most important lessons from Nexus is that the availability of information does not automatically make people better informed.

We often assume that access to more facts, news and opinions will help us understand the world more accurately. However, information can also be misleading, incomplete or deliberately manipulated.

Throughout history, information networks have helped societies organise themselves, preserve knowledge and cooperate on a large scale. Yet the same networks have also spread myths, propaganda and misinformation.

Harari explores this tension through historical examples ranging from religious institutions to modern political systems. The same challenge exists today. Social media allows us to access information within seconds, but it can also expose us to misleading headlines, unverified claims and content designed to provoke emotional reactions.

The lesson is to become more thoughtful about the information we consume. Instead of believing something simply because it appears frequently online, examine the source, look for supporting evidence and consider alternative explanations.

What to remember: Being informed is not just about knowing more. It is about learning to distinguish reliable information from misleading narratives.

2. The stories we believe shape society

Human beings depend on shared stories to build communities, establish institutions and coordinate their actions. These stories can include national identities, cultural traditions, political ideologies and ideas about how society should function.

In Nexus, Harari examines how information networks help these shared narratives spread across generations and large populations.

Such stories can bring people together around common goals, but they can also reinforce divisions when people accept different or conflicting versions of reality.

Consider how a single event can be interpreted differently by different communities. The facts may overlap, yet people's beliefs, experiences and sources of information can lead them to completely different conclusions.

Understanding this helps explain why disagreements are not always resolved by presenting more facts. Sometimes, people are also defending a larger story about their identity, values or place in the world.

What to remember: Question the narratives that influence your thinking. Understanding why you believe something is an important step towards forming independent opinions.

Also Read
6 Books that teach lessons from ordinary everyday life

3. Information is closely connected to power

Information has always been an important source of power. Those who control how information is collected, recorded and distributed can influence public opinion, shape decisions and determine which perspectives receive attention.

Harari traces this relationship through historical examples, examining how empires, religious institutions and political regimes have used information networks to maintain authority or influence society. He also considers how modern information systems affect the distribution of power.

Today, this relationship extends to digital platforms, search engines and algorithmic systems that determine what people see online. The information presented to us can influence what we consider important, which issues we discuss and how we understand current events.

This does not mean every information system is deliberately manipulative. Rather, it highlights the importance of asking who controls a system, what incentives shape it and whose interests it serves.

What to remember: Whenever information influences an important decision, consider who created it, who distributes it and who benefits from the way it is presented.

4. Artificial Intelligence makes information networks more complicated

Artificial intelligence is one of the most significant themes in Nexus. Harari explores how AI differs from earlier information technologies and why systems capable of generating content and making decisions could change the way information networks operate.

Unlike traditional tools that primarily store or transmit information, AI systems can generate persuasive text, images and other content at enormous scale. They can also perform tasks that previously required human judgement, raising questions about accountability and control.

These developments create opportunities in areas such as education, research and healthcare. At the same time, they raise concerns about fabricated information, automated manipulation and the difficulty of identifying who is responsible when AI systems cause harm.

The lesson is not to reject technology outright. It is to recognise that technological progress needs to be accompanied by critical thinking, appropriate safeguards and clear accountability.

What to remember: AI can help us process information, but we should not automatically treat its outputs as accurate or allow automated systems to make consequential decisions without appropriate oversight.

5. Human responsibility matters more than technological progress alone

A central concern in Nexus is that technological advancement does not guarantee that societies will make wise decisions. Humans have developed increasingly powerful tools and information networks, but the consequences depend on how these systems are designed, governed and used.

Harari argues that the future of information networks is not predetermined. The choices made by individuals, institutions and governments can influence whether new technologies strengthen society or create additional risks.

This is particularly relevant as AI becomes more integrated into everyday life. Decisions about privacy, misinformation, automated systems and the concentration of technological power will affect how people interact with information in the years ahead.

Responsibility therefore cannot rest entirely with technology companies or governments. Readers, citizens and technology users also have a role to play by checking claims, recognising uncertainty and thinking carefully about what they share.

What to remember: Progress is not simply about developing more powerful technology. It is about making responsible choices about how that technology affects human lives.

Final thoughts

Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI explores how information has shaped human civilisation, from shared beliefs to artificial intelligence.

The book argues that more information does not always mean more truth or wisdom. For readers navigating social media, digital news and AI-generated content, it highlights the need to question claims, examine evidence and think critically about how information shapes decisions.

item.title: Workflow, ecosystems, AI: Test your business creativity with Edition 255 of our weekly quiz!

item.content:encoded:
Lateral Sparks, the weekly quiz from YourStory, tests your domain knowledge, business acumen, and lateral thinking skills (see the previous edition here). In this 255th edition of the quiz, we present issues tackled by real-life entrepreneurs in their startup journeys.

What would you do if you were in their shoes? At the end of the quiz, you will find out what the entrepreneurs and innovators themselves actually did. Would you do things differently?

Check out YourStory’s Book Review section as well, with takeaways from over 355 titles on creativity and entrepreneurship, and our weekend PhotoSparks section on creativity in the arts.

Q1: Weeds

Most weeds in farms are currently removed manually or eliminated via spraying of pesticides, both of which are time consuming. What are some better ways of removing weeds?

Q2: The sports ecosystem

Sports and fitness for many people are moving past occasional events to a frequent, daily household habit. Where is the broader business opportunity here?

Digital tools help simplify digital advertising. But in a fast-moving and tech-immersed world, the broader question is how to improve marketing. Where is the business opportunity here?

There are many companies producing hydrogen fuel, with others manufacturing hydrogen-powered vehicles. But how will vehicles effectively get access to hydrogen fuelling infrastructure?

Many tasks require precise, repetitive movements, often in hazardous conditions. How can robotics be speeded up here to enable operations across diverse contexts and inputs?

Answers!

Congratulations on having come this far! But there’s more to come – answers to these five questions (below), as well as links to articles with more details on the entrepreneurs’ solutions. Happy reading, happy learning – and happy creating!

A1: Weeds

Founded by Rahul Arepaka and George Mathew, Harvested Robotics is building RAKSHAK, a tractor-mounted machine for de-weeding. It uses cameras to identify weeds and lasers to burn them as the tractor moves through a field.

Computer vision models help distinguish weeds from crops, and the onboard computer enables operation without an internet connection. Read more here about how this Tech30 startup's device can remove upto 100 weeds a minute for crop farms of potatoes and cauliflowers.

A2: The sports ecosystem

Founded by Pallav Bihani, Boldfit is a sports brand capitalisng on the fundamental shift in how people are engaging with fitness and sports. Its offerings include sportswear, gym equipment, fitness accessories, nutritional supplements, and wellness products.

It has invested in product innovation, manufacturing excellence and nationwide retail to serve India’s sporting ambitions at scale. Read more here about its fundraise from Wealth Company Alternates and Bessemer Venture Partners.

Founded by Karthik Venkateswaran, Nandha Kumar Ravi, Sundar Natesan, and Mukund Srivathsan, Zocket leverages AI for consumer brands. It has built a context and orchestration layer for AI-native marketing.

This helps in understanding the broader context of the brand, consumer and business setting and making that intelligence available across marketing workflows. Read more here about how it works with enterprise brands across 25 countries, with investment from Kalaari Capital and Kettleborough VC.

A4: Hydrogen fuel

Founded by Akshay Muley, Tejas Dattatray Chikhale and Nilesh Jadhav, Hyperonic Engineering is building indigenous hydrogen refuelling infrastructure, starting with gas dispensers. The founders have extensive experience in hydrogen production, fuel cells, and high-pressure gas systems.

Its flagship product is a hydrogen gas dispenser designed for refuelling stations. Read more here about its roadmap, and how it has received Rs 50 lakh support through the Startup India Seed Fund.

Founded by Abhit Kumar and Cameron Norris, Integra Robotics is building modular robotic hardware and software. It begins by allowing operators to control machines remotely, and then gradually automate more of their work.

The software operates in three modes: teleoperation, supervised autonomy, and fully autonomous operation. Read more here about its Indian patent for the teleoperation system, and its fundraise from Inflexion Point Ventures, India Accelerator Fund, and GrowthCap Ventures.

item.title: Art and design: how this award-winning Bengaluru airport elevates passenger experience
item.description:
As an eco-conscious terminal designed with lush garden-themed architecture, Terminal 2 at Bengaluru's Kempegowda International Airport has won much acclaim. This year, it was recognised among the Top 5 globally in the Skytrax rankings for World’s Best Art in the Airport.
This distinction undersco
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,020 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

As an eco-conscious terminal designed with lush garden-themed architecture, Terminal 2 at Bengaluru's Kempegowda International Airport has won much acclaim. This year, it was recognised among the Top 5 globally in the Skytrax rankings for World’s Best Art in the Airport.

This distinction underscores the airport’s systematic approach to integrating art within its architectural and operational framework. Curated works are not treated as standalone displays, but as integral components of the passenger journey.

With a conscious focus on showcasing the local art of Karnataka, the airport also positions itself as a dynamic, living museum. As shown in this two-part photo essay, cultural narratives and spatial design converge to create an immersive experience for travellers.

"Art and culture were conceived of as an integral part of the four pillars of design, along with Terminal in a Garden, Sustainability, and Technology," Yamini Telkar, Art Programme Advisor for Bangalore International Airport Limited (BIAL) tells YourStory.

The Art Programme serves as a cultural gateway to seamlessly integrate art with infrastructure. "This creates an immersive passenger journey centered on two primary themes: Karnataka's rich heritage and culture, and the Naurasa or nine emotions from Bharata's Natyashastra," she adds.

Also Read
How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups

The Art Programme was formally launched on September 8, 2023. Today, the airport showcases over 300 artworks by more than a hundred artists in the arrival and departure sections of the domestic and international terminals.

Featured artists include Vivek Matthew, Ganesh Shankar, Dinesh Maneer, LN Tallur, Madhvi Subrahmanian, Yayati Godbole, Sakshi Gupta, and dozens of others. Their diverse works span paintings, installations, mixed media works, sculptures, and digital displays.

"Over 90% of the artworks have been commissioned specifically for the Art Programme. Institutional partners are the Department of Archaeology Museums and Heritage, as well as the Museum of Art and Photography," Telkar explains.

Airports are more than transportation hubs; they are the first and last impression of a destination, and a defining part of the travel journey. Yet, for many passengers, the airport experience is shaped by queues, wayfinding challenges, crowded spaces, uncertainty, and long periods of waiting.

Art and design can transform the airport from a place passengers simply pass through into a place that welcomes, inspires and connects with them, as shown in this photo essay. Integrating creativity into the airport environment can make journeys more engaging and memorable.

Human-centred design, clear wayfinding, intuitive layouts, and accessible signage can ease passenger navigation. Terminal 2's flight information displays even include suggestions for passengers to check out art installations, depending on time available.

Also Read
Year in Review: The great Indian consumer reset powered by protein, pickleball and micro-dramas

Use of natural materials, biophilic design, daylight, greenery, and calming colour palettes can make terminals feel less stressful. Art, immersive installations, and the sound of flowing water can soften the intensity of busy environments.

Integration of local art, crafts, architecture, materials, stories, and cultural references give passengers an authentic sense of place. Terminals can become cultural showcases that offer visitors a meaningful introduction to the region and also instill pride among local residents.

For example, the Bengaluru airport features live performances during festivals. A six-day cultural celebration marked Naadahabba Dasara this week, with live music, dance, traditional crafts, games, and culinary experiences.

Art works across the span of the airport can create memorable moments along the entire passenger journey. This also makes the airport experience shareable and unique via organic word-of-mouth communication.

At the same time, it is important to ensure that creativity enhances usability rather than distracting from essential passenger information. This balance has been judiciously considered in the design of Terminal 2.

For BIAL, Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) led the overall architecture and interior design. "However the schematic and placement of the artworks was planned by the art team," Telkar explains.

Also Read
Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025

The identity of Bengaluru is reflected right from the concepts for the entry gates. "They showcase the verdant greenery of Bengaluru and Karnataka in the form of backlit photographs, which were specially commissioned," she describes.

Inspired by the Naurasa of the Natyashastra, the airport's Art Programme interprets the nine fundamental human emotions through a range of artistic expressions. The emotions are love, laughter, sorrow, anger, heroism, fear, disgust, wonder, and peace.

The collection of artworks at the airport has been developed through a combination of open calls, partnerships, loan programmes, patronage, commissions, and art-led events. This multi-layered approach allows the programme to bring together diverse artistic voices and practices.

The art experience extends outside the airport as well. In the arrival plaza, passengers and visitors are treated to a spectacular installation called Bengaluru's Soul, by renowned Catalan artist Jaume Plensa.

The sculpture has a number of interwoven figures. They evoke the collective human capital that powers Bengaluru’s rise as a global technology and innovation hub — distinct individuals, but unified in purpose, imagination, and inquiry.

In sum, art and design are not merely aesthetic enhancements; they are strategic tools for airport performance and differentiation. They improve the entire travel experience, and even nudge passengers to choose specific terminals and airlines for their travels.

Also Read
Year in review: What 2025’s data tells us about women in India

Distinctive design and authentic artistic expression help airports establish a recognisable identity in an increasingly competitive market. Public art and local creative partnerships strengthen cultural connections and support creative talent via airport displays.

Airports should certainly be secure and efficient places to travel through. But they can also offer cultural mearning and local resonance, as shown in this photo essay.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at BIAL.)

item.title: Comm min identifying AI-proof professions, sectors where India can take global lead: Goyal
item.description: The commerce and industry minister said that the focus would be on sectors where AI could improve efficiency without necessarily replacing human workers, while leveraging India's large pool of skilled talent, youthful population and traditional strengths.
item.content:encoded:
The commerce ministry is identifying professions less vulnerable to artificial intelligence (AI) to prepare for a fast-changing technological landscape and seize opportunities for India to emerge as a global leader, Union Minister Piyush Goyal said.

The commerce and industry minister said that the focus would be on sectors where AI could improve efficiency without necessarily replacing human workers, while leveraging India's large pool of skilled talent, youthful population and traditional strengths.

"I got my ministry to start working on what are the AI-proof professions. After all, we have to plan as a nation for so many millions of people. What are the sectors where AI can at max add to efficiency, not necessarily replace (human workforce)," the minister said on Friday while addressing Indian science and technology researchers and students in Germany.

When asked about the initiative's objective, he said India could take global leadership in several areas, including handicrafts, handloom, culinary arts, and tourism, by leveraging its vast pool of skilled talent and youthful population.

In these sectors, traditional skills and human creativity remain important, he said.

"... our handicraft, handloom... no amount of AI can replace that. So there are many, many areas where I think we have some very special strengths which we will be focusing on, also simultaneously developing, to ensure that 1.4 billion people have a better life in the future," he added.

Asked whether the government planned to offer incentives to these sectors, Goyal said it would provide support where necessary, but incentives wouldn't be required for every activity.

"It'll be a mix of several initiatives, some privately led, some government led, some people led, some opportunity led," he said, adding the broader objective was to develop India's strengths and create opportunities that would help improve the lives of its 1.4 billion people.

Goyal also talked about exploring ways to attract Indian researchers, engineers, and scientists working abroad to return and contribute to the country's development.

"I've asked them (the researchers and students here) to tell us what they will need to consider (the idea) and how we can support more young researchers or our talented engineers and scientific community to come and work and serve in India," he said.

Goyal said his discussions had highlighted that attracting talent was not merely a question of financial incentives, but also of creating a supportive environment for research and innovation.

"And surprisingly, I realise it's not just about money; it's about the enabling environment, the support of the ecosystem. So I (will) talk to my colleagues in the government, with educational institutions, both in the government and private sector, with academia, with leading research institutions in India, and industry, to see how we can forge industry, academia, and researchers partnerships," he said.

Referring to future global growth prospects, Goyal said developed countries would increasingly need to engage with emerging economies in Asia, Africa and Latin America, as these regions would drive future growth.

There are about 330,000 people of Indian origin in Germany, plus nearly 60-70,000 students.

"This large Indian student community, full of enthusiasm, seems to be very excited about taking their learnings back to India. Now we can see them not just looking for a job in Germany, but wanting to be back home to contribute to the India growth story, because that is where the action is," Goyal told reporters.

item.title: Will take action if Kannadigas sidelined in jobs in Karnataka: CM Shivakumar
item.description: In a post on 'X', Shivakumar said the government had taken concerns about Kannadigas being overlooked seriously and asserted that their rights, dignity, and opportunities would not be compromised.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar said on Sunday that the state government would take appropriate action if private institutions were found deliberately sidelining Kannadigas in job opportunities.

In a post on 'X', Shivakumar said the government had taken concerns about Kannadigas being overlooked seriously and asserted that their rights, dignity, and opportunities would not be compromised.

"It is disheartening to hear complaints that Kannadigas are being denied job opportunities in Bengaluru's IT companies. The government has taken seriously the issue of native Kannada speakers being sidelined," he said.

"In Karnataka, the Kannadiga is sovereign. The government will not allow the rights, dignity, and opportunities of Kannadigas to be disregarded for any reason," he said.

Noting that Bengaluru was recognised globally as India's technology capital, he said the state took immense pride in the talent, skills and capabilities of Kannadigas.

"If it is found that any private institution has deliberately sidelined Kannadigas, the government will take appropriate action," he said.

He emphasised that the government remained committed to addressing concerns relating to the interests of Kannadigas.

item.title: Startup funding falls below $100M; Deeptech startups look to go global
item.description: Venture capital funding in the third week of October recorded a sharp fall due to lower number of deals and absence of large value transactions.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

The AI boom is fuelling a datacentre expansion, but local communities are pushing back. In the UK, residents are raising concerns about noise, pollution, and blocked sunlight, putting the spotlight on the environmental costs of powering the AI revolution. With hundreds of facilities planned across the UK, the debate over who benefits and who bears the cost is growing.

Meanwhile, two critical PHP vulnerabilities exposed millions of websites and servers to potential cyberattacks. The flaws, undetected for years, triggered an urgent patching exercise, with experts warning that AI could make it easier to uncover and exploit similar weaknesses.

On the AI front, Block, a fintech company co-founded by Jack Dorsey, has unveiled Dessa, a voice model that captures human nuances such as laughter and pauses. It can listen and speak simultaneously and run on consumer-grade hardware, but is being tested by AI safety researchers before wider release. 

In other news, five companies are set to launch IPOs between October 26 and 29, aiming to raise nearly ₹2,600 crore, while Swara Baby Products, backed by FirstCry parent Brainbees Solutions, is among the other companies in the IPO pipeline and is expected to announce its launch plans by November 5. The upcoming issues come amid strong primary-market activity, with 104 companies raising over ₹1.4 lakh crore through IPOs so far in 2026.

In today’s newsletter: 

  • VC funding falls below $100M amid lack of big deals 
  • Experts urge deeptech startups to go global  

Here’s your trivia for today: What two-word term describes the total greenhouse gas emissions associated with a person, product or activity? (Scroll down for the answer)

Funding

VC funding falls below $100M amid lack of big deals

Venture capital funding into Indian startups fell sharply in the third week of October, as deal activity slowed and large-value transactions remained scarce. Startups raised $96 million across 15 deals, down from $180 million the previous week. With large funding rounds still limited, the ecosystem will be hoping for a revival in 2027. 

Key takeaways: 

  • Indian startups raised $96 million across 15 deals, marking the eighth time this year that weekly VC funding has fallen below the $100 million mark.
  • Even  Healthcare raised $50 million from Khosla Ventures and Alpha Wave, accounting for the largest deal of the week.
  • There have been just 16 funding deals worth $100 million or more in 2026 so far, highlighting the challenges startups face in securing large cheques.

TechSparks

Experts urge deeptech startups to go global

India’s deeptech ecosystem is gaining momentum, backed by improving government support, policy initiatives, and access to capital. However, talent shortages, funding gaps, and weaknesses in the manufacturing ecosystem remain challenges. At TechSparks 2026, industry experts said Indian deeptech startups must build self-belief and pursue global markets to scale.

Key takeaways: 

  • Government initiatives and funding are creating a more enabling environment for deeptech startups, but access to patient capital remains a challenge.
  • Startups need stronger engineering talent and a clearer focus on building foundational capabilities to strengthen India’s deeptech ecosystem.
  • Government procurement can provide an initial boost, but startups must look beyond India to build globally competitive deeptech businesses.

News & updates

  • Kannadiga jobs: Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar said the state government would take action if private institutions were found to be deliberately sidelining Kannadigas in hiring.
  • Starlink Restrictions: Elon Musk confirmed that SpaceX restricted Ukraine’s Starlink service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues had been resolved. He accused Ukraine of breaching its terms of service by using Starlink for military activity, while denying responsibility for a simultaneous issue with the US military’s Starshield system.
