item.title: Why India’s flying taxi revolution begins with electric air ambulances
item.description: Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Professor Satya Chakravarthy explained how The ePlane Company plans to avoid deeptech traps by launching high-margin electric air ambulances before scaling low-cost urban air taxis globally.
item.content:encoded:
For most deeptech entrepreneurs, the hardest lesson is not solving complex physics but overcoming their own technical fascination. Professor Satya Chakravarthy, Founder and technical lead of The ePlane Company, explained this clearly at TechSparks 2026, YourStory's flagship event.

“The biggest challenge that a deep tech entrepreneur normally would face is what I call the technology trap,” he said. “We have to actually ask the question who cares, and the moment you actually ask the question who cares... even your wife doesn’t care.”

Chakravarthy, an aerospace professor at IIT Madras, founded the company to develop electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs. These are battery-powered flying vehicles capable of hovering, taking off, and landing vertically without a runway. 

In a sector often driven by academic prestige, Chakravarthy insists that financial fundamentals must lead engineering ambitions. For deeptech startups, companies built on breakthroughs in science and engineering, long development timelines and heavy capital commitments mean that technological novelty alone cannot survive. 

In aerospace, he notes, becoming a unicorn is merely the minimum baseline, and founders must build business cases capable of reaching decacorn scale through healthy revenues and margins.

The inspiration for ePlane stemmed from a visit to Toulouse, France, where Chakravarthy discovered that 50 smaller aircraft manufacturers existed alongside global giants. 

“If there are 50 plane companies in France, maybe plane making is not so difficult... why don’t we give a shot at it?” he recalled. Coming from an academic institution accustomed to international standards, he aimed to build a world-class aircraft directly out of India.

The air ambulance strategy

To avoid the economic traps that have sunk rival aviation ventures, ePlane has designed a phased commercial rollout. Instead of launching directly into intracity air taxis, which represent a high-volume but low-margin business, ePlane is prioritising electric air ambulances. Emergency medical transport offers higher profit margins at lower production volumes, providing early positive cash flow while supply capacity scales up.

This approach also solves the challenge of demand modulation, preventing consumer frustration when early aircraft supply is limited. “First of all don’t let the bubble grow in the first place... be realistic about what is the customer that you can actually cater to,” Chakravarthy explains. 

Deploying five air ambulances in a congested city like Bangalore transforms emergency healthcare without overwhelming fleet capacity. Only after establishing economic stability will ePlane expand into short-haul air cargo and urban air taxis, where commuters can achieve a five-to-eightfold reduction in travel time for roughly double the cost of an Uber ride.

Global standards, Indian economics

Crucially, Chakravarthy rejects the notion that Indian innovations must settle for discounted quality. Because gravity and flight dynamics are identical everywhere, aircraft must satisfy rigorous international regulatory benchmarks, such as those set by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation. 

Building to global safety standards while keeping production costs low creates a distinct export advantage. As Chakravarthy asserts, “what’s good for India is good for the world.”

Engineering decisions at ePlane have been tailored specifically for practical certification and urban operation. The team deliberately avoided the tilt-rotor mechanism, a design where propellers rotate between vertical hover and horizontal flight, because single points of mechanical failure complicate regulatory approval. Instead, they selected a multi-rotor layout backed by redundant systems to ensure a straightforward path to certification. 

Public anxiety regarding urban air mobility is often misplaced when compared to everyday transit risks. Aviation regulators demand a failure rate of less than one in a billion before granting commercial approval. 

“If you are driving a car, you are actually driving something that can kill you... planes are much, much safer,” Chakravarthy remarks. Furthermore, by engineering the smallest aircraft footprint in its class, ePlane ensures its flying vehicles can land on existing hospital helipads and urban rooftops, including Metro station plazas.

With commercialisation targeted for 2028, ePlane represents a critical test case for the maturing Indian deeptech ecosystem. While government grants have provided crucial runway, private venture capital continues to struggle with long development cycles. “Patient capital still is more or less an oxymoron,” Chakravarthy reflects. 

Yet by pairing aerospace innovation with disciplined business strategy, India’s deeptech sector is proving that moonshot technologies can land firmly on commercial ground.

Cybercriminals wasted little time turning a software disclosure into an opportunity. Cloudflare detected millions of attempts to exploit vulnerabilities in PHP soon after they were made public, underscoring how quickly attackers can move to target exposed systems. The surge in attacks  has renewed concerns about the security of widely used systems and the urgency of patching vulnerabilities before they can be exploited.

On the jobs front, India’s healthcare global capability centres (GCCs) are expected to create 67,000 job openings in 2026, according to a Quess Corp report. Demand for specialised talent across technology and healthcare operations is expected to support this growth, reinforcing the sector’s shift towards more technology-driven work.

item.title: How art festivals benefit when galleries across cities collaborate
item.description: Our second photo essay from the Contemporary Now art festival in Chennai, and artist insights.
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,020 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

Chennai recently hosted the art festival 'Contemporary Now' spread across 10 venues in the city. The third edition of this festival included exhibitions, panel discussions, and curated walkthroughs in a number of galleries.

The diversity of artworks on display was testimony to the collaborative effort involving galleries from other Indian cities as well. Galleries from Kolkata, Ahmedabad, New Delhi, and Mumbai shared their art works for the Chennai festival.

The participating galleries included Experimenter, Archer, Vadehra Art Gallery, Ojas Art, Art Alive, TARQ, Chatterjee & Lal, Chemould Prescott Road, and Project 88. They represent different dimensions of India's art landscape: preservation of traditional practices, historically significant modern art programmes, and experimental contemporary practices.

Founded in 2009 by Prateek and Priyanka Raja, Experimenter is a contemporary art gallery with spaces in Kolkata and Mumbai. It is known for its intellectually ambitious and experimental approach to art, engaging with themes such as identity, politics, history, memory, and social change.

Beyond exhibitions, Experimenter supports critical discourse through artist talks, workshops, and publications. Its annual Curators’ Hub encourages emerging curatorial talent.

Also Read
How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups

Established in Ahmedabad in 1978, Archer Art Gallery grew out of an atelier founded by artist Anil Relia. It is particularly recognised for its work with limited-edition prints, including serigraphs of prominent Indian artists.

Founded in New Delhi in 1987, Vadehra Art Gallery is a leading institution for modern and contemporary South Asian art. It has played a significant role in supporting celebrated Indian modernists such as MF Husain, SH Raza, and Tyeb Mehta, and in art scholarship through its publishing programme.

Ojas Art was established in New Delhi in 2006 by Poonam and Rajiv Sethi, with a distinctive focus on India's indigenous, folk and tribal artistic practices. The gallery seeks to bridge the gap between traditional art forms and contemporary audiences.

Founded in New Delhi in 2001 by Sunaina Anand, Art Alive Gallery promotes modern and contemporary Indian art. It has also organised exhibitions of Indian art in international cities, helping introduce Indian artists to overseas audiences.

TARQ was founded in Mumbai in 2014 as a contemporary gallery for research-driven and experimental approaches to art. Its name, derived from the Urdu word tark, means logic or reasoning, and reflects its interest in encouraging critical engagement with art and ideas.

Established in Mumbai in 2003 by Mortimer Chatterjee and Tara Lal, Chatterjee & Lal spans contemporary art and design. The gallery combines solo exhibitions with research-based group shows that place artworks within wider historical, cultural and artistic contexts.

Also Read
Year in Review: The great Indian consumer reset powered by protein, pickleball and micro-dramas

Founded in 1963 by Kekoo and Khorshed Gandhy, Chemould Prescott Road is one of India's pioneering modern and contemporary art galleries. It champions experimental and interdisciplinary artistic practices, presenting works that range from painting and sculpture to photography and contemporary media.

Established in Mumbai in 2006 by Sree Goswami, Project 88 presents experimental and conceptually driven work by Indian and international artists. It often engages with challenging subjects such as globalisation, political structures, social inequalities, identity, and the relationship between art and public life.

Featured artists from many of these galleries and other institutions in Chennai are showcased in this photo essay. The lineup includes Jitish Kallat, Atul Dodiya, Shakuntala Kulkarni, Mithu Sen, Mohit Shelare, Reena Saini Kallat, Desmond Lazaro, and NS Harsha.

An art festival rooted in one city can thus become much more than a local cultural event through such collaboration. It transforms the festival into a meeting point for diverse artistic practices, regional identities, new perspectives, and creative communities.

Art does not exist in isolation, and neither should the platforms that showcase it. When galleries across cities come together, they create opportunities for artistic discovery and a stronger, more connected art ecosystem.

Audiences gain access to work they might not otherwise encounter, making the festival richer and more engaging. For emerging artists especially, these connections for broader exposure can be transformative.

Also Read
Year in Review: Top 10 celebrity-backed ventures of 2025

When a city welcomes artistic voices from elsewhere, it reinforces its position as an open, dynamic and culturally relevant destination. Gallery networks can continue long after the festival ends, creating ongoing opportunities for cultural exchange and professional growth.

When art travels, perspectives expand, and when galleries collaborate, opportunities multiply. Inter-city collaborations strengthen the entire art ecosystem of the country, in addition to promoting local artists.

One of the notable exhibitions at 'Contemporary Now' was titled How Long Will We Live? Or When Will We Die? It featured the works of Benitha Perciyal, and offered a comprehensive insight into her artistic practice built over three decades.

"I do not expect everyone to understand the work immediately. I simply hope they spend time with it. If they slow down, observe carefully, and begin asking their own questions, then the work has already begun its conversation," she explains.

"For me, that conversation is more important than providing fixed answers," she adds. As a mixed-media artist, she works extensively with wood. 

She also offers words of advice for aspiring creators. "Artists should listen to the world and listen to themselves as well," she tells YourStory.

Also Read
Year in review: What 2025’s data tells us about women in India

"Share what you want to say. Don't be too fast or harsh in judging the work of others and your own work," she adds.

It is also important to remember to pause often. "Reflect on your progress, process it, and accept that things may always be the way you want," Perciyal signs off.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at 'Contemporary Now' venues in Chennai.)

item.title: Five IPOs to open next week; companies eye close to Rs 2,600 Cr
item.description: The five upcoming IPOs will open for subscription between October 26 and October 29, offering investors exposure to sectors such as alternative investments, polymers, steel processing, wastewater treatment and jewellery retail.
item.content:encoded:
Five companies, including EAAA India Alternatives, SFC Environmental Technologies, and M K Sons Fine Jewels, are set to launch their initial public offerings (IPOs) next week, aiming to raise nearly Rs 2,600 crore in the primary market.

BLS Polymers and Bombay Coated and Special Steels would also float their maiden public offerings during the week.

Separately, several other companies, including Gujarat Victory Forging, Milestone Gears, Avaada Electro, Swara Baby Products, Integris Medtech and AGS Health, are in the pipeline for IPO, according to merchant bankers.

These companies are expected to announce price band declarations and launch plans by November 5, ahead of the extended Diwali holiday period in Gujarat, where markets and business activity are likely to be affected by the post-Diwali observance of Labh Pancham from November 6 to 15, they added.

The upcoming issues follow a busy month for the primary market, which saw Jio Platforms launch the country's biggest-ever public issue worth Rs 30,213 crore.

As many as 104 companies have raised over Rs 1.4 lakh crore through IPOs so far in 2026, suggesting continued primary market activity.

The five upcoming IPOs will open for subscription between October 26 and October 29, offering investors exposure to sectors such as alternative investments, polymers, steel processing, wastewater treatment and jewellery retail.

These offerings are expected to keep the primary market active as companies tap investor demand to raise funds for business expansion, working capital requirements and debt repayment, while some existing shareholders seek to monetise their holdings.

EAAA India Alternatives, an arm of Edelweiss Financial Services, will open its Rs 1,200-crore IPO on October 26 and close it on October 28. The company has fixed a price band of Rs 1,585-1,665 per share, valuing it at Rs 10,765 crore at the upper end.

The issue is entirely an offer for sale (OFS) by the Edelweiss Group, meaning the company will not receive any proceeds from the offering. EAAA India Alternatives has already raised around Rs 360 crore from anchor investors ahead of the public issue.

SFC Environmental Technologies, a wastewater treatment solutions provider, will launch its Rs 668-crore IPO, with the subscription closing on October 29. The company has fixed a price band of Rs 313-330 per share, valuing it at around Rs 3,233 crore at the upper end.

The issue comprises a fresh issue of equity shares worth Rs 150 crore and an offer for sale of up to 1.57 crore shares by promoters and existing shareholders. The company will use the proceeds from the fresh issue to repay debt and meet working capital requirements.

M K Sons Fine Jewels Ltd will open its Rs 275.4-crore IPO on October 28 and close it on October 30. The company has fixed a price band of Rs 153-162 per share.

The IPO comprises a fresh issue of 1.36 crore equity shares and an offer for sale of 34 lakh shares by promoter selling shareholder Ramchand Murlidhar Raimalani.

The jewellery retailer plans to use the net proceeds to fund inventory for setting up a new showroom in Maharashtra and expanding an existing showroom in Gujarat, repay or prepay certain borrowings, and meet general corporate expenses.

BLS Polymers Ltd will launch its Rs 255-crore IPO on October 27, with the issue closing on October 29. The company has fixed a price band of Rs 142-150 per share. The issue comprises a fresh offering of 1.7 crore equity shares.

The company plans to use Rs 77.56 crore of the proceeds to expand its manufacturing facility and increase production capacity, while Rs 89.5 crore will meet working capital requirements. The remaining amount will be utilised for general corporate purposes.

Bombay Coated and Special Steels Ltd will open its Rs 183.1-crore IPO on October 29, with the issue closing on November 2. The company has fixed a price band of Rs 78-82 per share.

The IPO will be an entirely fresh issue of equity shares. The company plans to use Rs 125 crore to repay or prepay certain borrowings and Rs 15.7 crore to finance the acquisition of capital equipment under existing lease arrangements with Siemens Financial Services. The remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes.

item.title: Deeptech startups in India must have global ambitions, urge panellists at TechSparks
item.description: Many aspects are falling in place for the growth of the deeptech ecosystem in India; startups must nurture self-belief and ambition in tandem, said industry experts at TechSparks 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The deeptech sector in the Indian startup ecosystem has emerged out of the shadows and carved a niche for itself. Many aspects are falling in place for the growth of deeptech startups, and despite various challenges companies from India must cultivate global ambitions, concurred experts at a panel discussion at TechSparks, YourStory’s tech-startup summit.

The panel comprised founders from the domains of robotics, precision manufacturing, and semiconductors, and an executive from a policy think-tank. The session was moderated by Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director - Strategic Content & Video, YourStory.

Despite the challenges in the sector, the panellists agreed that the overall environment was changing for the better.

Kaushik Mudda, Founder & CEO, Ethereal Machines, a high precision manufacturing startup, said, “We have most things in place that enable us to compete globally.”

According to Shweta Rajpal Kohli, President & CEO of Startup Policy Forum, the deeptech ecosystem has found its rightful place with the government making key contributions in terms of capital and policies. “I think the government's done a lot of things right in terms of providing that enabling environment. This is India's moment to push deeptech.”

Today, the deeptech sector is keen on building or possessing technologies that are critical to the sovereignty of the country.

Agnit Semiconductors’ co-founder and CEO Hareesh Chandrasekar said, “We need to build across the ecosystem but this will only be built over time.”

Agnit Semiconductors is India’s first vertically integrated gallium nitride semiconductor product startup.

Challenges in the sector

Commenting on the challenges that deeptech startups are facing in the country, Gokul N A, the founder of robotics startup CynLr said, especially in the space they are present in, the ecosystem is still absent. There is also a shortage of talent, especially at the mid-management level, he added.

“We don’t churn that much volume of quality engineers in the country as we are still very service oriented,” he remarked.

The panellists were of the view that the country needs to have clear focus areas in the deeptech segment, which is a fairly vast subject.

“We need to start building the basic building block of what it takes to become a manufacturing superpower,” Mudda said.

Chandrasekar remarked that, in the current environment where semiconductors have been weaponised, it is important for the country to develop sovereign capability.

Availability of capital is another roadblock, although the situation is much better now than in the past.

According to Gokul, while seed-stage funding has improved, a lot needs to be done to get patient capital into the segment.

Kohli said the capital challenge is being solved, especially with the government coming out with a Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation Fund.

Mudda opined that funding up to $5 million is not much of a challenge for deeptech startups but there is still a scarcity when it comes to the next level of fundraise—$10million to $15 million.

Deeptech needs a global market

On the government as a customer for deeptech startups in the country, the panellists said the government can be an enabler but startups should look at global markets.

“That demand generation and the government as the first buyer is a big boost for any sector,” said Kohli. But the government’s procurement process is a bit complicated, he added.

According to Chandrasekhar, while startups would like the government to be their first customer, it cannot be the only customer.

Deep technology needs a global market, and cannot have India alone as its focus, said Gokul.

According to Kohli, self-belief among participants in the ecosystem needs to improve to ensure deeptech grows bigger. “India has the talent, scale and everything going for it. We just need to accelerate it at a feverish pace now,” she remarked.
